claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy film can be deposited on a stainless-steel substrate by DC magnetron sputtering.
Applying a magnetron-sputtered refractory high-entropy alloy coating improves stainless-steel corrosion resistance relative to uncoated or conventionally coated substrates.
The stainless-steel substrate has a conventional passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer on stainless steel is susceptible to breakdown in extreme corrosive media.
Data-driven parameter optimization can guide tailoring of the sputtered refractory high-entropy alloy film.
Stainless steel typically loses performance in highly saline, acidic, or otherwise aggressive corrosion environments.
DC-magnetron sputtering can produce a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy layer on 304 stainless steel.
The sputtered layer is dense and uniform.
The nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy layer acts as a robust physical barrier to corrosive species.
The refractory high-entropy alloy layer lowers the diffusivity of corrosive agents.
Lower corrosive-agent diffusivity preserves substrate integrity and delays passivity breakdown.
The coating produces significantly lower corrosion current and improved passivation behavior.
The coating reduces corrosion rates by orders of magnitude relative to bare stainless steel.
Uncoated stainless steel typically undergoes localized pitting or general corrosion in aggressive media.
Sputtering power, substrate temperature, and gas flow must be controlled to obtain a uniform, defect-free coating.
Coating performance may vary at very high temperatures or under chemical exposures beyond tested regimes.
Quantitative corrosion data for the coating under varied operating environments are limited.
Extended electrochemical testing is required to establish real-world coating durability.
